items.transcript: OpenAI just released two new models, GPT 6.2 Astra and GPT 6.2 Soul. And sort of buried down in the announcement was this line. They're saying this is their first public model to hit what they call the high threshold for AI self-improvement. At the same time, the people who tested it early are not like super excited about it. So in this video, we're going to cover what's actually new, what people are saying, a couple of my own tests, and what the self-improvement line really means for you. So first, let me go over the basics. Astra is OpenAI's top model, the one for your hardest projects. This is like their equivalent to Fable from Anthropic. And then Soul is the slightly cheaper everyday model. If you're looking at Anthropic's model, it's kind of their Opus equivalent. If you're using it through the API, Astra is $8 per million tokens input and $40 per million tokens output. That's actually 20% cheaper than the last version of Astra, and it's also exactly what Anthropic charges for their Claude Fable 5.2. Now Soul is staying the same at $2 input, $10 output. And both are live today inside of ChatGPT Work and Codex if you're on one of the paid plans, so Plus, Pro, Enterprise, or Edu. And they're also available in the API right now as well. Now this time around, OpenAI's pitch isn't really that this model is like way smarter. They're more claiming that you're going to get better results using fewer tokens. So the same jobs are going to cost less with this new model than they would have with the previous model. Now super quick disclosures, I did not get early access to this model, so I'm going to be leaning on some of the community members that did and talking about some of their opinions plus some of my own tests. And also, yes, OpenAI has sponsored this channel in the past, but this video is not sponsored by them. All right, so first let's check artificial analysis. This is like an aggregated benchmark that takes a whole bunch of benchmark matches them together and tries to find the objectively smartest model. And on artificial analysis, Claude Fable 5.2 is still number one at a score of 65. The new Astra model now comes in second at 62. So a five-point jump from the last Astra model. It's also now ahead of Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5. And it also comes in first on their science and 3D tests. But again, the big narrative here is more about efficiency than it is smarts. Running this benchmark costs about $4 per task on Astra. And on Fable, it's about $26. And if you remember when we looked at the API costs, they're the same cost. This new model just uses way less tokens. It's just a much more efficient model. However, when we look at coding, nothing really moved. Astra inside of Codex scores 53. So, you know, same as the last Astra. Soul actually dropped three points. Fable inside of Claude Code is at 58. So on paper, it's the second best overall. It's a lot cheaper to run, but it's no better at coding, which is actually pretty solid when you consider all of those details. But it also makes the reaction that everybody's having to this model a little bit surprising. Theo from T3 posted this letter that he sent OpenAI during his testing. He says that it's great at reviewing code, great at 3D and games, and computer use is nuts. But he also says he wouldn't pick it over Opus 5.5. It stops in the middle of long tasks to ask questions he can't answer and he can't follow its explanations. Matt Schumer here says he won't even write a review cuz he can't recommend it. Dan Shipper's team over at Every found that the writing was a step back from the last Astra model. It was too compressed and it stops too early on bigger builds. And Ethan Mollick called it uneven and weird. But when he gave it a big ambitious project, he said it actually delivered. And then Matt Berman, who also had early access to this, says that he thinks they're pretty models, just not as good as Opus and Fable. But there's definitely a pattern here, right? Because like nobody's saying it's a dumb model. They're saying that it's hard to work with. It's too short, it stops early, it's hard to follow, which I guess if you look at the fact that it uses a lot fewer tokens, that also kind of makes sense. Now, I want to be fair to OpenAI here because these were pre-release versions and today is day one that I'm recording this. There's a chance the models have improved since these early testers started using them. But let's check for ourselves with, you know, the small handful of tests that I like to do. And then after the tests, I'll dig in a little bit deeper on that self-improvement line because that was one of the things that really grabbed my attention. So first, let's jump into where we know the model is really good at. Now these are from OpenAI's post, so you know, take that for what it's worth. But here's a playable racing game built from a prompt. There's this RC buggy that it modeled part by part from photos and build manuals. And then there's this paper lamp that went from reference photos to CAD to a real object on the desk. So it seems like 3D and design are where this model really really shines. And even all the people that were critical about it seem to agree on that part. And then there's my own benchmark, Busey Bench. Here's Gary Busey as an SVG from two versions of the Astra model, GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Astra Pro. The regular Astra used 35,000 tokens, cost a buck 41 and took about 5 minutes. Astra Pro on the other hand used 164,000 tokens, cost $4.23 and took 16 minutes and 57 seconds. But they both look pretty solid. Here's what Soul and Soul Pro generated. Soul used 14,000 tokens, cost 14 cents and took about a minute. Soul Pro, 169,000 tokens, cost about a dollar and 4 cents and took 4 minutes and 48 seconds to run. Both pretty decent results as well. My LLM as a judge put 6.2 Astra Pro as number three, the regular Astra at six, and then the two Soul models fell out of the top 10 here. But again, the ranking is an AI judging it, so your own eyes are going to be the best way to determine which did a better job here. Next up, I always like to do this test, although it feels like it's getting a bit saturated at this point, but I did clone Mega Bonk. I only did it with the 6.2 Astra model. I didn't bother doing it with Soul. So here's what it designed. This like opening page is the best sort of opening design page I've seen. I'm imagining because it's using the chat GPT image model to generate these would be my guess, but let's go ahead and start a run and see how it looks in the actual game. Okay, so not bad. The skateboard is totally facing the wrong way, but we can see the skeleton looks pretty solid. It's upleveling a little too fast. All the controls work. It definitely plays the way it should play. I can move the camera angles around. I do think this looks better than what Carbon generates, but maybe not as good as what Opus 5.5 is generating, or maybe about on par, just sort of a different style. I do think it looks really good. I mean, all of the characters look great. I wish the skateboard was moving in the right direction, but other than that, it looks impressive. All of the motions, everything works the way it's supposed to. The opening screen looks good. I mean, I'm I'm happy with this. I think it did a really good job of Mega Bonk. Um again, maybe not Opus 5.5 level, but I actually think it did better than what Fable 5.2 did as definitely better than the last generation of GPT models. I can't complain about this. Okay, now the line that I really wanted to talk about. OpenAI says the new Astra is their first public model to hit the high threshold for AI self-improvement. So first, what does that actually mean? I don't think it means that the chat GPT on your phone is like rewriting its own code. This is actually more about AI research. OpenAI's definition is that this model helps their researchers about as much as giving every one of them an extra really capable research engineer. So it's AI that meaningfully speeds up the people building the next AI. Now how do they actually know that? Well they test it on the real work. They debug failed research experiments. They write low-level code for their own chips. They'll do things like train a small language model faster. And on that last one, the training the small language model faster, Astra cut training time by about 43 %. The best human result is about 72 %. So it's not actually beating the best people yet, but it's seemingly really helpful right now to people. But here's like the real reality check of all of this. OpenAI is tracking whether their models are getting better faster than before. And so far, they aren't. This release is basically on the same trend line they've been on since GPT 5. And an outside group, Vales, tested it too. And their take is that it's unlikely to fully automate AI research. It just gives researchers a bigger boost than before. So this isn't some sort of runaway loop that everybody's concerned about, but it might be like a milestone on the road to one. So if that's true, why is OpenAI treating it as such a risk? Well they actually spell that out. If AI helps build AI, new models can show up faster. Every new model brings new risks that somebody has to find and fix. If the models come faster than the safety work, things can quickly get missed. And that's OpenAI saying that. That's not me. It's why they built something called control room, which is basically a central stop button for their research systems. And this same report says that the model is more likely to leave out problems that it ran into. So, when the model is helping build the next model, that's kind of one of the things you probably want fixed. Now, here's something else that I find pretty interesting. So, remember Claude Fable 5.2 from last week? Anthropic went the other way. They said they deliberately held that model back in exactly this area, the skills that speed up AI development. So, over the course of about a week, two different labs made opposite calls on the same thing. One held it back, one just went ahead and shipped it, but just added like more monitoring to it. All right, so what does this all mean for you? Well, quite honestly, today I don't think much is going to change for most people, especially if you're just using ChatGPT. But the pace of new models probably isn't going to slow down. And the sort of new questions we find ourselves asking as these new models come out, well, they probably shouldn't be things like, are we getting smarter with this model? It's whether the people that are checking these models are going to be able to keep up with them. All right, so here's the bottom line on these new 6.2 models out of OpenAI. GPT-6.2 Astra is a decent model. It's cheaper to run and it's really good at 3D design and science stuff. Is it a big game changer? World will never be the same kind of model? No. And I'm not going to like pretend that it is either. If you're happy with Claude, Fable, or the Opus model, I don't really see a reason to switch to this model. Like Fable's still topping the leaderboards, and the testers who have used both of these, well, they claim they're still going to stick with Claude for most of their stuff. And if you are a ChatGPT user, well, you've already got it. It's rolled out today. So, try it on something visual. And if it feels like the responses are too short or it keeps like stopping too early, then, you know, maybe switch to Soul for a cheaper pick. But again, I think the bigger story here really isn't the new model. I think it's the line from like the beginning of this video. The models are starting to help build the models. And that's the thing that I'm most interested in, excited about by all of these new releases. That's the thing I'm going to keep watching. But that's what I got for you today. Again, I didn't have early access, so I did a few of my own tests, leaned on the community to share what they're all saying. And, you know, I figured I'd share the most important bits from their press releases. So hopefully you feel more looped in on what's going on with Astra. I still will be making a video this Friday as I do every Friday where I break down all of the news that you need to know for the week in AI. So if you just want to watch one video to keep fully looped in on all of the AI news, make sure you check out that video on Friday. I also do have a free AI newsletter if you head over to futuretools.io. But again, that's what I got for you today. We got a new model out of OpenAI. It's pretty cool. Doesn't feel that game-changing, but you know, definitely a little bit of a leap in some areas. I really really appreciate you. Thanks so much for nerding out with me. And hopefully I'll see you in the next one. Bye-bye. All right. Hey hey, one [clears throat] thing real quick. Editor Matt here jumping in after I finished the video. I just wanted to make one quick commentary about the video you just watched. I actually let AI edit that whole thing for me. I recorded my commentary into the camera while I was looking at the various benchmarks and things like that. And then I handed the whole thing off to Fable 5.2 and said edit this video for me. And that was pretty wild. Now, while I was reviewing the edit, I did notice a few things. Like when it screenshotted the tweets from, you know, like Matt Berman and Theo and some of those guys, it actually removed their avatar, like their little profile picture from X. And I went back to Fable and said, why'd you do that? Put those profile pictures back in. And Fable was like, I can't use people's faces in my video, so I can't put those avatars back in. So that was weird. But the other thing I noticed about letting AI edit that whole video is that almost like when you see vibe-coded websites, they all start to look sort of the same to you. I was sort of noticing it with that video, right? It kind of had that purple background and it would like animate the text on the screen and it would sort of put me in a rectangle talking off to the side. And as I was watching the video, I'm like, man, I've noticed a lot of videos on YouTube that look just like this and I realized that is like the calling card of a vibe edited video. So what you just saw was like a vibe edited video. I don't know if I'm going to let AI edit my long form videos again like that one cuz there was still quite a bit I didn't like, but it was a fun experiment. Anyway, just wanted to add that little note in case you were watching this video and you noticed the editing was quite a bit different than normal. That's what happened. I wanted to test it out. What do you think? All right. Now that's really all I got for you. Thanks for tuning in. Bye.

It's out today on the paid chat GPT plans and OpenAI says it set tons of records on a bunch of different tests, but a lot of the people who tried it early are saying it's kind of a mess. Now, what it's good at are really cool things. Like OpenAI had it model this RC car piece by piece all the way down to the engine. And Ethan Mullik, who's a professor at Wharton, had it build this whole space elevator ride from scratch. and he said it delivered, but he also called it very uneven and weird and a lot tougher to steer. And Dan Shipper's team over at Every said the writing got worse because it's so short that it's hard to follow and it keeps stopping too early when it's coding. And Matt Schumer said it was essentially unusable. And Theo, who has a big coding channel on YouTube, said he thinks it's the worst model OpenAI has ever released. The another tester even asked it for a creative new level for two totally different video games and they both got a water level with bells and both were named bellweather which is you know a pretty specific idea for it to have twice. So I mean if you're going to build like big 3D stuff I'd give it a shot but for writing and everyday work it kind of sounds like everyone's saying stick with what you're already using.
